comparator.name: Chemistry
comparator.sourceNotes: The 180 EC degree includes 82.5 EC of required chemistry courses and thesis work, 52.5 EC of major electives, and 45 EC of profiling electives. This example includes electives from all three required subject groups.

routeSelection.basis: This example follows Utrecht’s Molecules and Materials direction, listed first on the student curriculum page. The chosen courses combine materials and physical chemistry with biochemistry, molecular modelling and structure determination.

core: Biomolecules, proteins, cells, biochemistry and molecular laboratory investigation
Materials behaviour, sustainable chemistry, lifecycle impacts, environmental biogeochemistry, energy and resource recovery
Experimental, laboratory, data and research methods for molecular, material and environmental questions
adjacent: Molecular disease mechanisms, medicines and therapeutic research
Mathematics, programming, data analysis and computational modelling for molecular and material systems

trace: develops a product concept, fabrication method and prototype and evaluates sustainability and cost; it supports chemical-product design questions without teaching chemical synthesis or process equipment
develops data cleaning, visualisation and analysis for experimental, environmental and materials data
supplies structured programming, testing and debugging for quantitative analysis and system models
introduces calculus, matrices, complex numbers and differential equations used in quantitative process and environmental models
teaches stable numerical solution methods for equations, interpolation, integration and differential equations
develops probability, distributions, estimation and simulation for experimental and model uncertainty
examines recycling, recovery and remediation technologies, resource security, inorganic chemistry and laboratory work for circular material systems
examines how public and private actors make and implement sustainability policy, a concrete institutional dimension of lower-impact industrial transition
uses field and laboratory analyses to study soil properties, remediation and aquifers as material and environmental systems
uses system modelling, proxies and isotope tracers to analyse linked Earth-system processes and greenhouse-gas pathways
studies aqueous and mineral biogeochemical processes, water treatment and resource recovery using geochemical modelling
conducts advanced research on resources, geothermal energy, carbon capture and waste storage
establishes physics, chemistry, materials, mathematics and modelling foundations for sustainability problems
uses waves, optical spectroscopy, electron microscopy, chemical testing and crystallography as introductory methods for sustainability investigations
examines climate drivers, impacts, mitigation, renewable energy and carbon storage as the context for lower-impact production
directly evaluates environmental impacts of products and processes across their lifecycle and develops circular-economy planning
assesses energy-use patterns and technically and economically evaluates solar, wind and bioenergy system designs
uses mathematical models and transforms to analyse linear systems and signals, supporting quantitative study of system response
introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells and DNA as a biological foundation for molecular and biotechnology questions
studies eukaryotic and prokaryotic cell biology and current life-science research methods
directly studies proteins, sugars, lipids, nucleic acids, metabolic pathways and biotechnology applications
provides biochemical and molecular laboratory work with proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics
studies molecular genetics, cell injury, inflammation, repair and disease as one health-facing application of molecular science
implements regression, classification, resampling and clustering for prediction and pattern discovery in molecular-life and biomedical data
develops matrix, vector and eigenvalue methods for multivariable biological and pharmacological models
studies disease frequency, risk, screening and causal evidence, supporting population-level assessment of therapeutic effectiveness and safety
connects anatomical structure with organ-system function and medical imaging, locating therapeutic action and disease effects within the human body
directly studies drug targets, molecular interactions, pharmacokinetics, toxicity and quantitative concentration-response relationships
studies immune recognition, host-pathogen interactions and immunopathology as disease mechanisms and therapeutic targets
derives pathophysiology across organ systems from anatomy and physiology, providing the disease-mechanism basis for rational intervention
studies neurobiology, disorders, animal models, laboratory techniques and research ethics as one concrete biomedical application domain
studies neural mechanisms of perception and action, supplying organ-system function relevant to neuroactive drug effects without claiming neuropharmacology
introduces brain and behavioural science plus experimental methods as the formal foundation for later treatment-evidence synthesis and neural applications
studies homeostasis, signalling and integrated organ-system physiology needed to understand drug effects in the human body
develops regression, multivariate analysis and experimental inference for biomedical and treatment-response evidence
performs systematic review and meta-analysis in R to estimate treatment effects and assess consistency across studies
supports academic planning, reflection and professional development throughout the programme

alternatives.label: Biochemistry, Materials and Sustainable Resources
alternatives.concept: Study molecules in living cells and in environmental systems. Connect biochemistry and lab work with soil and water chemistry, resource recovery and product life cycles. Use mathematics and data analysis to study these systems and evaluate renewable energy designs.
alternatives.labelReason: The label reflects the main subjects and methods of the selected courses.
progression: Life science foundations precede cell biology and biochemistry, which precede the life science laboratory. Sustainability Essentials I precedes II and the advanced environmental courses. Mathematical Methods precedes numerical methods, linear systems and probability.

alternatives.label: Molecular Life Science, Disease and Drug Research
alternatives.concept: Study how molecules and cells work, how disease disrupts them, and how drugs act in the body. Combine laboratory work, physiology, immunology and pharmacology with statistical analysis and research on treatment effects.
alternatives.labelReason: The label reflects the main subjects and methods of the selected courses.
progression: Life science foundations precede cell biology, biochemistry and physiology. Cell biology and biochemistry precede the life science laboratory. Biochemistry and physiology precede pharmacology. Experimental methods precede the advanced research seminar.
alternatives.distinctness: Thirteen courses (97.5 EC) differ in each direction. This plan studies drug action, immunity and disease mechanisms. The other plan focuses on environmental chemistry, resources and sustainable systems.

candidates.label: Molecular Life Science, Disease and Drug Research
candidates.assessment: Biochemistry and molecular laboratory work support a course sequence in cell biology, drug action and disease mechanisms. Physiology, immunology, pharmacology and treatment evidence give this plan a distinct focus.

candidates.label: Specialist molecular, reaction, analytical and laboratory chemistry
candidates.assessment: UCR offers useful foundations in biochemistry, data and numerical methods, and applied materials and chemical testing. A specialist direction requires linked courses in chemical synthesis, reaction mechanisms, spectroscopy, structure determination and physical chemistry, plus advanced chemistry lab practice. The selected workbook provides isolated elements of this sequence.

selection.assessment: The two UCR plans share a base in biochemistry and quantitative methods and differ by 97.5 EC each way. A dedicated chemistry plan would require a sequence in synthesis, spectroscopy, structure determination and physical chemistry with chemistry laboratory progression.

blocks: Biomolecules, cells, disease and therapeutic research
Both examine how the chemistry of biomolecules underlies life. UCR develops protein structure, enzyme action and metabolism.
Both develop experimental practice in the chemistry of living systems. UCR uses protein and molecular biology techniques in a life science laboratory.
Both develop calculus as a foundation for scientific work. Utrecht also covers mechanics, work and energy.
Materials, environmental chemistry, energy and resources
Chemistry specialisms, thesis and profiling electives
Utrecht links organic reaction mechanisms and synthesis with spectroscopy in the lab.
Utrecht applies thermodynamics and redox chemistry in chemical experiments.
Utrecht develops quantum models of chemical structure alongside inorganic chemistry.
Utrecht develops analytical chemistry techniques through lab investigations.
Utrecht studies the thermodynamics of real gases and liquids.
Choose profiling electives across the two slots, with at least 15 EC at advanced level in total for this selection.
Utrecht develops diffraction, scattering and imaging to determine molecular and material structure. UCR introduces crystallography and microscopy in sustainability.
Utrecht develops statistical thermodynamics and the study of colloids, polymers and interfaces.
Utrecht relates the physical chemistry of solids and surfaces to devices such as lasers and solar cells.
Utrecht requires a 15 EC chemistry thesis. UCR shows optional independent research separately.
Continue the 45 EC of profiling electives.
Utrecht uses protein function to explore advanced biochemistry in health and disease. UCR covers related cellular and disease processes in several courses.
Utrecht combines mathematics with electromagnetism. UCR studies matrices and related methods in its mathematics courses.
Utrecht applies mathematics to molecular modelling. UCR uses numerical methods to solve more general scientific problems.
Utrecht combines data analysis with spectroscopy and chemical structure problems. UCR studies general data analysis and introduces optical spectroscopy in sustainability.
Utrecht studies coordination compounds, solid-state theory and inorganic synthesis. UCR introduces materials and chemical testing in sustainability.

notes.text: The UCR plans share biochemistry, molecular laboratory work and quantitative methods. Utrecht develops a longer sequence in organic, inorganic, analytical and physical chemistry, with synthesis, spectroscopy and a required chemistry thesis.

audience.programmeDescription: Utrecht’s Chemistry degree studies how substances are structured, how they react and how to investigate them in the lab. First-year courses are mainly in Dutch, intermediate courses use Dutch and English, and advanced courses are taught in English.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The Utrecht example combines core chemistry with materials electives. The UCR options connect biochemistry with sustainable resources or with disease and drug research.
